title: Finance and the Sources of Growth
research_question: Does the level of development of the banking sector exert a causal effect on long-run economic growth, and through which channels — total factor productivity growth, physical capital accumulation, or private saving rates — does this effect operate?
data_description: The study assembles cross-country data covering up to 77 countries over 1960–1995, with observations either averaged across the full period (one observation per country, 63 countries) or averaged over seven non-overlapping five-year sub-periods for panel analysis. Key variables include real per capita GDP growth, per capita physical capital growth (constructed from disaggregated investment and depreciation data in Penn-World Tables 5.6 across five capital categories), and three measures of total factor productivity growth based on alternative aggregate production functions incorporating human capital (years of schooling from Barro and Lee). Banking sector development is measured by Private Credit (financial intermediary credit to the private sector/GDP), Liquid Liabilities/GDP, and the share of commercial bank assets in total bank assets, all carefully deflated. Private saving rates (gross private saving/gross private disposable income, 1971–1995, 61–72 countries) come from a World Bank database. Conditioning variables include initial GDP per capita, schooling, government size, trade openness, inflation, and black market premium.
institutional_context: The paper is motivated by a long-running debate in development economics between the Schumpeterian view, which holds that banks shape growth primarily by allocating savings to productive uses and thereby accelerating productivity and technological change, and the capital-fundamentalist view, which holds that financial development matters mainly through raising saving rates and capital accumulation. A related motivation is the renewed interest in explaining the large unexplained component of cross-country differences in total factor productivity. The institutional setting exploits the fact that countries' legal systems descend from one of four European legal traditions (English common law, French, German, or Scandinavian civil law) that were typically transplanted through colonization or occupation. These legal origins are documented to shape laws governing bank credit, contract enforcement, creditor protection, and accounting/disclosure standards, which in turn condition the depth and functioning of national banking systems.
